Q1: 
The paragraph logically opens with the competitive landscape (3) → AI adoption (1) → funding interest (2) → concerns (4).

Why the correct order is 3 → 1 → 2 → 4

1) Opener = 3

  • Role: Sets the context/problem: rising competition.

  • Logic: A good first sentence frames why the topic matters. “As competition intensifies…” naturally introduces the need for solutions.

2) Next = 1

  • Link to 3: Cause → Response
    From “competition intensifies” (3) to “adopting AI” (1) as the solution firms choose to gain an edge.

  • Flow device: “seek innovative tools” (3) → “adopting AI to automate & reduce error” (1) is a direct, specific instantiation of that search.

3) Then = 2

  • Narrative progression: After establishing adoption, we move to market consequences—specifically, investor behavior.

  • Coherence: It’s natural to go from firms adopting AI (1) to investors supporting scalable AI models (2).

4) Conclusion = 4

  • Why last: Starts with “However,” a contrastive connector that signals a caveat/closure point.

  • “Also” presupposes prior mention of AI use; it works best after we’ve discussed adoption and investment, not before.

  • Function: Provides a balanced concluding perspective by highlighting ethical risks.

Why? “Work in a coordinated manner” expresses organized teamwork, which is logical for achieving goals; the other options are negative or ill-fitting.

1. Key phrase: “completed … schedule” tells us the blank must express a time relation with the planned schedule.

  2. Collocations:

    • ahead of schedule → earlier than the planned finish date.

    • on schedule → exactly on time.

    • over schedule or beneath schedule → not idiomatic in this context (you’d say “behind schedule” or “over time”).

  3. Tone: The sentence says “remarkable progress,” implying faster completion than expected.

✅ Correct Answer: B) ahead of schedule

“Ahead of schedule” means finishing earlier than the original plan, matching the positive tone (“remarkable progress”).

Detailed Reasoning:

  • The subject is “The teacher” (singular).

  • The phrase “along with her students” is a parenthetical addition; it does not change the number of the subject.

  • Therefore, the verb must be was preparing, not were preparing.

✅ Correct sentence: The teacher along with her students was preparing for the annual function.

• When two subjects are joined by neither … nor …, the verb agrees with the nearest subject (the one immediately before the verb).

    • If the nearest subject is singular, use singular verb.

    • If the nearest subject is plural, use plural verb.

Why part 3 is wrong

  • Here the two joined subjects are: “the manager” (singular) and “his assistants” (plural).

  • The verb must therefore agree with the nearest subject to the verb — i.e., “assistants” (plural). So the correct verb is were, not was.

  • Thus part 3 (“was willing to accept”) contains the error.

Correct sentence:

  • Neither the manager nor his assistants were willing to accept the responsibility.

Short examples to remember

  • Neither the coach nor the players were ready. (players = nearest → plural)

  • Neither the players nor the coach was ready. (coach = nearest → singular)

  • Neither the cat nor the dogs are outside. (dogs nearest → plural)
